summaries.example: You look outside and see a wet sidewalk, so you believe it rained. But imagine a special machine made the sidewalk look wet even though it is dry. Your eyes would seem to give the same message in both cases. Philosophers ask whether the first belief is still well-supported and how we could tell the difference.
summaries.summary: This entry asks a big question: how can seeing, hearing, and touching give us knowledge about things outside our minds? A skeptical argument says that our experiences might be misleading. A dream or a brain-in-a-machine story could produce experiences just like ours while the world is very different. Philosophers respond in several ways. Some say perception puts us directly in contact with objects. Others say that perceptual beliefs can be reasonable because experiences support them, because the process that formed them is usually reliable, or because the person is genuinely connected with the world. The entry explains that no single change in the story automatically settles every question. We must also ask what makes a belief justified and how perception supports it.
key_ideas: Our senses usually seem to teach us about objects outside our minds.
A skeptical story can make our experiences seem unreliable: a dream, a trick, or a brain connected to a machine might feel just like ordinary life.
Some philosophers change their picture of perception and say that the world is directly present to us.
Other philosophers focus on rules for good belief, such as evidence, reliable processes, or a real connection with the world.
Changing the picture of perception may not solve every question about whether our beliefs are justified.
summaries.why_it_matters: We depend on perception every day, from crossing a street to learning about science. Thinking carefully about perception helps us understand why ordinary beliefs can be sensible, how mistakes are possible, and why doubt about the outside world is such a deep philosophical problem.

important_terms.definition: Knowledge or belief that has good support or reasons behind it.
Doubt about whether we can know things outside our own minds.
The things outside our minds that we try to see, hear, touch, and learn about.
A way of reaching something through another thing that may sometimes mislead us.
A belief that has support without needing support from another belief first.

questions_to_think_about: If a dream feels exactly like waking life, what could show that you are awake?
Does seeing a red apple give you a reason to believe an apple is really there?
Can a belief be reasonable even when it turns out to be wrong?
Which seems more important: having good evidence, using a reliable way of forming beliefs, or actually seeing the thing?

summaries.example: Suppose two people have the same visual experience of a chair. One is really looking at a chair; the other is hallucinating because of a vivid dream or an unusual device. An internalist theory may say that the experience itself gives both people some initial justification. A world-involving theory may say that the successful perceiver has a special kind of justification because the actual chair is part of the perceptual relation. The disagreement concerns whether justification depends only on the subject’s experience or also on the world.
summaries.summary: The epistemological problem of perception concerns how perceptual experience can justify beliefs about a mind-independent world. PEW presents the challenge in three steps: perception supplies only appearances; justified belief requires a reason to regard those appearances as accurate; and no non-question-begging reason seems available. If the argument succeeds, ordinary perceptual beliefs would not be justified. Metaphysical theories respond by rejecting or revising the first step. Idealism closes the gap between appearance and world by treating ordinary objects as mental, whereas direct realism makes perception a relation to mind-independent objects. The entry distinguishes several senses of “direct,” since a theory may make judgment noninferential without making perception world-involving or justification basic. Epistemological theories address the other steps. Classical foundationalism demands metaevidence, while modest foundationalism and seemings internalism allow perceptual experience to provide prima facie justification directly. Coherentism appeals to mutually supporting beliefs; etiological theories appeal to reliable or properly functioning belief-forming processes; and world-involving theories give veridical perception a distinctive evidential status. The source emphasizes that metaphysics alone does not settle the epistemology, and that these approaches can sometimes be combined.
key_ideas: The central skeptical argument, PEW, moves from indirect access, through a demand for evidence that appearances are accurate, to the conclusion that perceptual beliefs are unjustified.

Metaphysical responses challenge the account of what perception is. Idealism treats ordinary objects as mental constructions or collections of experiences, while realism treats them as mind-independent.

“Direct presence” has several meanings: noninferential judgment, direct reference to objects, unmediated perception, world-involving experience, and justification that is not based on other justification.
Epistemological responses challenge the evidential requirements instead. Foundationalists, coherentists, and defenders of seemings offer different accounts of how perceptual beliefs gain support.
Etiological theories appeal to the origin of a belief, such as a reliable cognitive process or proper function, rather than requiring an accessible reason.
World-involving theories distinguish genuine perception from hallucination by giving the veridical case a special connection to the perceived object.
summaries.why_it_matters: Perception is a main route by which people form beliefs about reality, so its epistemology affects knowledge in science, everyday reasoning, memory, and testimony. The debate also clarifies the difference between being right, being justified, and knowing. It shows why skeptical scenarios are powerful while also explaining why rejecting skepticism requires more than simply insisting that perception feels trustworthy.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of whether perceptual beliefs are justified or count as knowledge.
The claim that perception gives the mind only appearances, not unmediated access to external objects.
The requirement that one must have reason to think an appearance is accurate before relying on it.
The claim that we lack such a reason, creating a skeptical challenge.
A view that some beliefs are justified without depending on support from other beliefs.
A view that justification can arise from mutual support among beliefs rather than from basic beliefs.
A view that perceptual belief can receive initial justification from how things seem, without prior evidence that perception is reliable.
A view that perceptual justification depends on an appropriate relation to the actual world or truthmaker.

questions_to_think_about: Does a theory of what perception is by itself explain why a perceptual belief is justified?
If an experience is the same in a real and hallucinated case, should it provide the same justification in both?
Can a belief be justified by a reliable process even when the person cannot explain why that process is reliable?
Does coherent support among beliefs need some connection to perception in order to avoid becoming a well-organized fiction?
Would a person who has no experience but forms accurate perceptual beliefs through a reliable process have justification?

summaries.example: Imagine that your phone shows a weather picture saying it is raining. You normally trust the picture because the phone has worked well before. But suppose the same picture could be produced by a glitch while the sky is sunny. You might ask whether the picture itself gives you a reason, whether the phone’s history makes the belief reasonable, or whether you need some direct connection to the actual weather. Perception raises a similar question about seeing the world.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how perception could justify beliefs about an external, mind-independent world. A skeptical argument begins with the thought that we encounter appearances rather than objects without mediation. It then adds that we need a reason to believe these appearances are accurate, followed by the claim that any attempted check would rely on further perception and risk circularity. The conclusion is that perceptual beliefs are not justified, and therefore may not be knowledge. Philosophers challenge this argument in two broad ways. Metaphysical approaches revise the nature of perception: idealism treats ordinary objects as mental constructions, while direct realism makes perception an unmediated relation to external objects. The source carefully separates several meanings of directness, including noninferential judgment, direct reference, unmediated awareness, world-involving experience, and basic justification. Epistemological approaches instead revise the standards for justification. Classical foundationalism requires support for the reliability of appearances; modest foundationalism and seemings internalism allow experiences to provide initial support without such prior evidence. Coherentism emphasizes mutually supporting beliefs, reliabilism emphasizes reliable belief-forming processes, and world-involving views emphasize successful contact with the truth. The entry concludes that a satisfactory response must explain both the nature of perception and the epistemic principles governing perceptual belief.
key_ideas: Skeptical scenarios do not merely say that we sometimes make mistakes. They ask how we could rule out a situation in which our experiences are systematically misleading.
The main skeptical argument depends especially on two claims: we need reasons that appearances are accurate, and we do not have such reasons without using perception again.
Some philosophers try to solve the problem by changing the metaphysics of perception. Others change the rules they think justification must follow.

“Direct perception” can mean different things. A judgment may happen without conscious reasoning, refer to an outside object without referring through another object, or involve the perceiver and world in a direct relation.
Different epistemological theories emphasize evidence, the history of belief formation, or the believer’s actual contact with what makes the belief true.
A metaphysical theory may weaken skepticism without proving that perceptual beliefs are justified; an account of justification is still needed.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters whenever we ask whether our senses are trustworthy and what makes a belief reasonable. It connects everyday mistakes with large skeptical possibilities, and it helps distinguish several questions that are often mixed together: what perception is, why a belief is justified, whether it is true, and whether it amounts to knowledge.

important_terms.definition: A belief is justified when it has enough support to be reasonable, even if it later turns out to be false.
The view that we may be unable to know whether the world outside our minds is really as it appears.
The idea that mental appearances stand between us and outside objects.
A philosophical argument claiming that perceptual beliefs lack justification if appearances might be misleading.
A theory saying that some beliefs have justification without depending on other justified beliefs.
A theory saying that beliefs can support one another as a connected system.
The idea that a belief is justified because the process producing it usually leads to truth.
A kind of perception whose justification depends on an actual relation between the perceiver and the world.

questions_to_think_about: Is using past successful experiences to defend perception circular, or can it be a legitimate argument?
Should a vivid hallucination give someone the same initial justification as a genuine perception?
What is the difference between a belief being true by luck and being formed by a reliable method?
Can several beliefs support one another without any of them having a special starting point?
Which meaning of “direct” seems most important for solving skepticism: direct access, direct reference, or direct justification?
